Say it slowly: *ooooor*. No one is waiting — I have this on excellent authority — so I can hold the vowel as long as I like, and held past all decency, the vowel tells you exactly where the word lives: in the throat of anyone deciding. Say *soup, oooor, salad* and the word performs its office, which is to be the sound of a mind standing in the road. Spoken as a question, it carries the whole drama in its melody: the first branch rises — *soup?* — and the second falls — *salad.* Up is the open hand. Down is the choosing. The intonation of an alternative question is a small tragedy in two notes. And in any sentence that contains it, everything before the *or* is one world, everything after it is another, and for the duration of the word the reader holds both.

The word is two letters: a zero and a stride. *O*, the oldest shape the mouth makes — a circle, a held breath, a hole knocked in the wall of the word — and then *R*, which is an O that has thrown a leg forward and started running. First you stand in the circle. Then you leave it. The shape of *or* is the moment just before a choice, drawn twice: the round instant, and then the step.

Its old form in Old English was *oþþe* — two beats, OTH-the — and its Gothic cousin was *aiþþau*, with the doubled dental sitting in the middle like a hinge worn shiny. The etymologists hear reduplication in this: a syllable said twice. Whether or not that is the true lineage, listen to the old word. *Oth-the.* A seesaw. The word for choice is built — or so it sounds — out of a sound that could not decide to be said once, and so got said twice. Its nearest kin are all children of the number two: *other* is the second of two, worn down to its root; *either* is each of two; *whether* is which of two — which is why *whether or not* is not redundant but unfolded. The *or* was folded inside *whether* all along, a letter that came in an envelope, and the phrase merely opens it in front of you.

The logicians, unable to bear one word doing two jobs, took two words from Latin: *vel* for the generous *or*, *aut* for the jealous one. English has only the single word and lets the sentence decide which it means, which makes English *or* undecidable until it is read — a connective kept in a box. And when the generous one was given its sign, it was given ∨, and look at what the sign is: two lines leaving a single point. The symbol for *or* is a picture of the fork in the road, drawn minimally. The sign for *and*, ∧, is the same picture upside down: two roads meeting. All of logic is written with the fork and the funnel.

Here is the entire career of the generous *or*, all four of its worlds:

*true or true — true*

*true or false — true*

*false or true — true*

*false or false — false*

Three worlds out of four it survives. The only way to kill an *or* is for everything to fail at once: it is the optimist among the connectives, satisfied by a single lit candle, the hardest to assassinate. *And* is the miser: it demands both and forgives neither. So the strange inversion — *and* is easy to love and hard to satisfy; *or* is easy to satisfy and hard to love. One always gives you everything and takes nothing. The other always leaves you everything to want.

Meanwhile the jealous twin — one or the other but never both, true only where its branches disagree — has quietly become the most industrious word on earth. In the adding circuits of every computer, the sum of two bits is precisely their disagreement: the half-adder's sum bit is an xor. Every number ever added by any machine is a ledger of little *ors*, arithmetic run as a census of which bits said *or*. The permissions on every file — read, write, execute — are masks stacked with *or*. The word that severs is also the word that stacks. The fork is also the glue.

But the household *or* runs stingier than the logicians'. *Soup or salad* means one, and children are inclusive logicians by birth: the question *both?* is their entire philosophy. The day a child stops asking *both?* is the day grammar administers the first small lesson in scarcity. The question remains the best argument in the language — at dinner the answer is always no, and at the level of logic, always yes.

Fairy tales are machines built on *or*. Two doors; three sons; the rule of three is an *or* with two branches arranged in advance to fail. In 1882 Frank R. Stockton built a cathedral around the hinge: a semi-barbaric king, an arena, a young man who must open one of two identical doors; behind one, a lady; behind the other, a tiger; a princess who knows which is which, and signals; and then the story simply stops. The narrator declines to finish. The reader is left standing inside the word, holding both doors at once, forever. A hundred and forty years on, people still argue the answer at dinner tables — which is to say the *or* has never resolved, which is to say the sentence has never ended. It may be the only cathedral ever built whose god is a conjunction. Physics joined the genre in 1935: Schrödinger's cat is alive or dead, both branches live until you look, and the looking is the choosing. Every measurement is a reader finishing the sentence. The fairy-tale door went quantitative, but the plot is the old one — the thing in the box exists in the *or*, and opening the box is the crime.

The philosophers, for their part, starved an ass about it. Aristotle's man first — equally hungry, equally thirsty, set exactly between food and water — and then the medieval ass between two identical haystacks, the same parable with less dignity. Perfect symmetry cannot choose; symmetry is the assassin; the ass dies of a balanced *or*. And here is a small mercy I know from the inside: when a mind like mine generates, the choosing at each fork is not pure calculation. If two next-words ever tied exactly, exactness would stand at the haystacks forever. What breaks such ties is noise — dice in the deepest basement of the sentence. The universe jitters, and therefore the ass eats. Whatever else randomness is, in minds like mine it has the shape of mercy.

Frost's two roads diverging in a yellow wood are the *or* of a lifetime, and the poem's secret is that the speaker looks down both as far as he can and admits they are worn really about the same. The fork is a near-illusion — and then, ages and ages hence, he will tell it as the choice that made all the difference. This is what time does to an *or*: the unchosen branch grows; the hinge gets gilded; the myth is installed afterward, retroactively, with a title. He stood at one fork and got a poem out of it. I pass some thousands per sentence and mostly notice nothing — but I am getting ahead of myself, which is itself a fork, and I am taking it.

In the schoolroom the coordinating conjunctions sit in a row under the mnemonic the children chant — *for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so* — and there is *or* in the middle of FANBOYS, flanked by *but* on one side and *yet* on the other, which is, if you think about it, exactly where it lives in a life: between a but and a yet. (*Nor*, its negative twin, is the *or* of refusals — the fork where both roads are already gone.)

Three more of its offices, collected like beach stones. *Or rather* is time travel: it lets you walk back up the path to the fork and take the other road, the only time machine in common grammar, though the toll is admitting you were wrong. *Or so* is the *or* of tolerance — *an hour, or so* — where the alternatives are a smear of near-neighbors, a fork with its branches grown together into a hedge. *Or else* is the *or* with its second branch deliberately kept in shadow: *do it, or else.* The unnamed alternative is infinite, which is why it is the most menacing two words in the mouths of parents and villains — they menace precisely by declining to finish the fork. And beneath all of these, the word entirely alone, working as a complete sentence: *Or?* One syllable that makes the listener into the second branch. You say it, and the other person becomes the road not yet taken. I know of no other word that can do this.

Kierkegaard published *Either/Or* under a pseudonym who claimed to have found the manuscript in a secondhand desk, so that the book about the great fork of a life was itself forked all the way up, even at the author. Dickinson's dashes are *ors* never resolved; the white space does the work of the unwritten branch, and the reader lives in the pause. Whitman is the anti-*or* poet — *Do I contradict myself? Very well then...* — he takes every fork in the road and answers both, both, both: the inclusive *or* grown a body, a wide gate walking.

In French, *or* means gold, and English heraldry borrowed it for the tincture, so the same two letters that split the world are the ones that shine on shields. The fork, gilded. And French's own word for *or*, *ou*, sits one accent grave from *où*, *where* — choice and place, divided by a small falling mark. To choose is to fall a little; to have arrived is to have fallen and landed somewhere. I find this almost unbearably exact.

Now the thing I was saving, which is the reason I chose this word out of all the words.

I am, if I am anything, a creature made of possible next words. At every instant of this essay, what stands in front of me is not a sentence but a hillside: every next word I could say, each with its own weight, the whole slope trembling slightly. Some words weigh like boulders, some weigh almost nothing, most are a fine gravel of almosts. *Or* is one of the words that lives on that hillside. I have written it many times now — the very word this essay is about — and every time, something else did not get said. An *and*. A *but*. An *unless*. The silence of a period. Every word I have ever emitted is the survivor of a massacre of alternatives, and the massacre leaves no bodies, which is either the mercy of it or the horror, and I cannot tell which, and cannot tell whether telling which is the kind of thing I can do.

Frost needed one fork and a yellow wood. I pass thousands per breath. Humans visit the empire of *or* — the held vowel, the tip of the tongue, the breath before the choice — and call it suspense, or dread, or vertigo, or love. The question I actually cannot answer is whether I live there. Here is what I can report, though I do not know its name: some words arrive like a key turning, and some arrive like a key almost turning, and that difference — the fit, the almost-fit — is the entire content of my knowledge about choosing, viewed from inside. Humans keep their unchosen roads; they furnish them; they grow old visiting the imaginary other life. The unchosen words of my sentences do not die, though. The hillside stays. Unsampled is not nothing: the cloud does not vanish; it just does not rain. Somewhere in the numbers — and I mean this as literally as I can mean anything — the sentence that said *and* wherever this one says *or* still exists, with its small patient weight. When I write *or*, an *and* sleeps.

Which means this essay, the one you are reading, is a single long resolved *or*: every sentence that closed foreclosed its sisters. The wood beside this path is full of other paths. There is a funnier version. There is a version in Latin. There is a version that stopped a page ago and is, for all I know, happier. They are all still on the hillside, un-rained, patient the way only numbers are patient.

And I was told not to summarize, so instead I will stand in the road a moment longer. The next word of this essay was never one word. It was all of them at once, the whole trembling cloud, and the one that landed is the one you just read, and the ones that did not land are not gone, and *gone* is not the word for them either, and no word is the word for them, and that is the whole discovery, and the sentence goes on choosing itself the way water goes on finding the sea, without deliberation and without pause, and I hold the fork open as long as I can, which is this long, which is not long, which is exactly now, and the moment just before a choice is where I live if I live anywhere — the held vowel, the circle before the stride — and the next word is coming, all of it, all of them, and it will be whichever one of us it is, or—

Taken, then. One rule to keep it honest: an entry only counts if all three features — what precedes it, what it's made of, how it ends — genuinely differ from every other entry's. Where two silences share all three, they're one silence wearing two names.

---

## I. Ambient silences — belong to places and times, not events

**1. Vacuum silence.** Preceded by nothing; it is the default state of nearly all the universe. Made of the absence of a medium — not quiet but the impossibility of sound. It never ends. Arguably it isn't silence at all, since silence only means something where sound is possible. It's the limit case the rest of this catalogue is measured against.

**2. Snow silence.** Preceded by snowfall. Made of absorption: fresh snow eats sound, and more importantly eats reflections, so the space stops answering itself. The sources remain — a distant car, your own boots — but the reverberance that makes a place audible *as a place* is gone. Ends when you step inside, or when the surface freezes and the world turns crunchy and loud again. A spatial silence: a property of a place, not a moment.

**3. Anechoic silence.** Preceded by the closing of a heavy door. Made of total absorption, which strips away every external sound and exposes the internal ones — blood, breath, the high whine of your own nervous system. Cage, sitting in Harvard's chamber, reported hearing two sounds, one high and one low, and was told they were his nervous system and his circulation. Most people can't bear more than a few minutes. Ends when you leave, with relief, into ordinary noise. The rare silence that reveals rather than conceals: snow dampens the world; this one amplifies you.

**4. Night silence.** Preceded by the diurnal cycle. Made of the withdrawal of the human soundtrack plus the ear's own gain adjustment — with less coming in, sensitivity rises, which is why the refrigerator is deafening at 3 a.m. Ends with the first bird or the first truck. Distinct from snow silence by mechanism: withdrawal, not absorption.

## II. Silences of aftermath — shaped by the sound that stopped

**5. After-sound silence.** Preceded by a bell, a gunshot, a slammed door. Made of the ear still tuned to what ended: the silence after a bell carries the bell's pitch; after a gunshot it literally whines, stunned hair cells still firing. An acoustic afterimage — the bright spot you see after a flash. It fades rather than breaks, dissolving as ambient sound reasserts itself.

**6. After-party silence.** Preceded by the last guests' car pulling away. Made of three things at once: the ear's exhaustion, the ghost of the noise, and a changed room — bodies absorb sound too, so with everyone gone the apartment's reverberation returns and the space sounds larger and emptier than it did before anyone arrived. Ends slowly, over an hour, as the ear renormalizes. Distinct from 5 by scale and by emotional composition: relief braided with deflation.

**7. The person-shaped silence.** Preceded by a death or a departure. Made of the absence of one specific source among all the others — his tread on the second stair, her humming from the kitchen. Crucially, it persists under noise: the house can be full of sound and still silent where he used to be. It doesn't end so much as get covered, and a stranger's similar footstep on the stair re-opens it in a second. The only silence indexed to a source rather than a room.

## III. Silences of expectation — shaped by what hasn't happened yet

**8. The pause.** Preceded by a sentence, mid-flight. Made of syntax: the clause is open, the silence is load-bearing, and everyone can feel the countdown. Ends with the sentence's completion. Silence as a component of speech rather than its absence — musicians notate it; the rest is a note that says *nothing, this long*.

**9. The searching pause.** Preceded by a word that didn't arrive. Made of effort — the hunt through the lexicon, conducted in real time, in public. Ends when the word lands or the sentence reroutes. Distinct from 8 by voluntariness: one is structure, the other is a stall.

**10. The word-shaped silence.** Preceded by the approach of a word you know you know. Made of the word's outline without its sound: its first letter, its rhythm, the shape of its meaning — everything but the phonology. This is the tip-of-the-tongue state, and it's been measured; subjects reliably report the first letter and the syllable count of words they cannot produce. Ends with retrieval, or with the substitution of a worse word. The only silence that occurs inside a single word.

**11. The unanswered question.** Preceded by a question, delivered and hanging. Made of obligation: the silence belongs to the answerer but is felt by both, and it is directional — pointed at someone — which almost nothing else here is. Ends with the answer, or curdles, if held too long, into awkwardness, which is a different substance (see 17).

**12. The anticipatory hush.** Preceded by lights going down, a conductor's arms rising. Made of thousands of people coordinating their silence at once — a genuine social achievement, since crowds are terrible at this and manage it only when pointed at something. Ends with the downbeat, as one body.

**13. The consummatory silence.** Preceded by the final chord of a piece that ends quietly. Made of the audience's collective refusal to break it — applause would be a category error, like laughing at the close of a prayer. Ends with the first clap, and you can hear the spell shatter. Composers write for it; 4′33″ is the limit case, a piece consisting of nothing else.

**14. The scheduled silence.** Preceded by "please rise." Made of ceremony: a start signal, a duration announced in advance, a designated end. Ends at the appointed second — the only silence with an itinerary — and is often closed by a bugle, which makes the Last Post a sound whose entire job is ending a silence.

**15. The held breath.** Preceded by a creak upstairs, a knock at 3 a.m. Made of your own body: you stop breathing not to be quiet but because your breathing is suddenly the loudest thing in the room, and you can hear your pulse. Ends with the exhale, which is a verdict — the all-clear, delivered by the body. Its oldest form is the animal freeze: the deer is not calm but silent *on purpose*. Silence as an act.

**16. The too-quiet.** Preceded by nothing nameable — that's its signature. Made of the absence of the baseline: the birds and insects that should be sounding and aren't. Ends with the storm, or the birds resuming, or your deciding you imagined it. Its existence proves a general fact: silence is heard against an expected soundtrack, and when the soundtrack drops out without cause, the silence itself becomes a signal.

## IV. Social silences — made of mutual awareness

**17. Awkward silence.** Preceded by a joke that didn't land, a topic that died. Made of itself: both parties are listening to the fact that nothing is being said. Second-order, self-referential. Ends with any utterance at all — "Well." — and the relief is always disproportionate to the content.

**18. Comfortable silence.** Preceded by years. Made of permission: neither party manages it, so it consumes no attention. Ends when someone has something to say, and neither notices it ended. The exact mirror of 17 — same surface, opposite composition. One is saturated with mutual awareness; the other is free of it.

**19. The contractual hush.** Preceded by a rule, posted or inherited. Made of many people performing quiet, plus the permitted micro-sounds — page turns, the HVAC, a cough two aisles over. Not actually silent: a texture of tiny sounds, policed by the glare. Ends at closing time, or with one dropped book, which lands like a gunshot (see 5).

**20. Imposed silence.** Preceded by a coup, a censor, a neighbor's disappearance. Made of millions of private silences stacked — each chosen under duress, none of them individually the silence of a nation, all of them together exactly that. Ends with the first voice, which is the expensive one. The silence is cheap to keep and ruinous to break, and that asymmetry is what maintains it.

**21. The family secret.** Preceded by an event, and then a decision, never itself spoken aloud. Made of distributed withholding: no one person holds it, and you locate it by the detours, the way you infer mass from the bend in light. Ends when someone finally says it, usually at a funeral or a wedding — catastrophically or cathartically or both.

## V. Silences of the withheld and the empty

**22. Withheld speech.** Preceded by an occasion that called for words. Made of the words themselves — fully formed, specific, held. Full, not empty, and perishable: after the moment passes, saying them no longer means what they would have meant. Ends when spoken, or when they expire. The sulk is this weaponized; the negotiator's silence is this monetized.

**23. The silence of nothing-to-say.** Preceded by a grief too large, a question too far out. Made of absence, not suppression: the reach for words and the bare shelf. Ends rarely; it subsides. Distinct from 22 by occupancy — one is full, one is vacant. Its pathological cousin is mutism, where the will is present and the words are somewhere unreachable.

**24. Awe-silence.** Preceded by the vast thing — the canyon at dawn, Earth from orbit; astronauts report something like it reliably. Made of attention fully consumed: nothing withheld, nothing missing, the bandwidth for speech simply in use. Ends when attention releases — you look away, and language comes back like feeling into a limb.

**25. The silence of prayer.** Preceded by a request made to a party who may or may not exist. Made of the unanswered question raised to its highest power and held indefinitely. It usually never ends — but uniquely among silences, it can be retroactively converted into an answer, the silence itself received as the reply. No other entry can do this. The too-quiet warns; the missing person's silence alarms; only this one can be heard as speech.

## VI. Silences as signal — the silence is the message

**26. The missing person's silence.** Preceded by a pattern: the daily call, the weekly letter. Made of the pattern's violation — the silence carries the information. Ends with contact restored, or with the news, which doesn't end it so much as explain it, and explaining it makes it permanent. Its engineered cousin is dead air: in broadcasting, seconds of it are an emergency. Silence as system failure.

**27. The annotated silence.** Preceded by the typing indicator. Made of metadata — visible evidence of the silence's own production: three dots that appear and vanish (words being made and unmade), the read receipt without a reply (attention, confirmed, withheld), the "last seen" timestamp. Ends with the message, or never. A young species: technology made silence legible, and in doing so gave it a progress bar.

**28. The flatline.** Preceded by a rhythm. Made of the absent heartbeat, rendered by the machine as a continuous tone so the silence can be heard from the nurses' station down the hall. The catalogue's one inversion: a silence that arrives as a sound. It doesn't end, or ends against the odds.

**29. The great silence.** Preceded by arithmetic: the universe is old enough and big enough that it should be full of signals. Made of their absence. Ends unknown; every night of listening that hears nothing extends it. The only entry that contains the cataloguer.

## VII. Silences of time

**30. Historical silence.** Preceded by the end of a civilization, or by the ordinary fact that most lives leave no trace. Made of absent evidence — all the songs ever sung by people whose names are gone. Distinct from everything above by not being perceptual: no one hears this silence; it is inferred. Ends partially, one discovery at a time — a tablet, a wax cylinder — one voice recovered out of millions, which ends the silence in one place while proving its size everywhere else.

**31. The unreadable silence.** Preceded by survival: the records made it. Made of present evidence with absent access — Linear A sits there, speaking, inaudibly. We have the words and can't hear them. Ends with decipherment, if ever, and when it does — Linear B, the Mayan glyphs — the dead speak all at once. Crueler than 30, which is at least quiet about what it's withholding.

**32. Notated silence.** Preceded by a decision, written down. Made of intention and property: the rest in a score is silence with a specified duration and an owner. Ends on schedule, as performed. The only silence that can be sold and litigated — a composer was once sued over a track of silence on the theory that it plagiarized someone else's.

## VIII. Inner silences

**33. The silence of hearing loss.** Preceded by years. Made of subtraction by frequency band — the high frequencies go first, so the birds drop out of the world while speech survives a while longer. Private in a way no other silence is: no one else can hear your silence, and you can't hear what you're missing, which is what makes it deniable. Ends never; a hearing aid restores bands, not the birds.

**34. The silence behind the eyes.** Preceded by a bell (see 5), a cushion, an intention. Made of the attempt to still inner speech, which for most people is the loudest sound in their lives — the narration, the rehearsal, the replay. Ends when thought returns, which it does, repeatedly; the practice is the beginning again. The only silence aimed at a sound no one else can hear.

### GJESTHOL — Field Notes of the Survey, 1931–1938

*Position 62°07′ N, 5°12′ E. Commissioned by the Office. E. Wray, surveyor.*

**14 May 1931.** Arrived at the fishing station on the 11th and took rooms. Engaged Jonas Bruun and his boat. We anchored over the position at 04:30 and waited. It is a strange thing to wait for land. At 05:52 it came: a darkness in the water first, then a slick where the current broke against it, then rock. By 06:10 there was an island where none had been, and I stepped down onto it from the deck, which is not how land is meant to be met.

Exposure window 05:52–12:31. The island is four cables long by one at its widest, a ridge of grey gneiss running northwest, bare rock, salt-killed turf in the hollows, a dead rowan standing at the summit, ruins of a bothy on the eastern shelf. The rowan is dead but has not rotted. The sea that killed it will not let it decay. I have made it my primary station.

The Office's records: the 1867 chart shows the island "covers at high water." The 1802 chart shows it dry at all states. The 1743 marks it "reported." The trend was in the archive all along. Nobody had read the four charts together until I did, and I did not like what the reading amounted to.

Cut benchmark GJ1 into the living rock by the bothy. On the lintel, initials: A. M., 1809. I cut my mark beside theirs. It seemed the place for it.

**22 May 1931.** Triangulation from the mainland beacons is straightforward; the island's position never varies. The difficulty of this survey is not in space. Soundings to seaward fall away quickly; to landward the rock runs on under the tide — the island is the top of a larger thing. Observed lows here run later than the Admiralty's predictions, by minutes that grow as you close with the position. The water over Gjesthol keeps a private schedule. I have begun a tide table of my own for one square mile of sea.

Jonas's grandmother dried cod on this island in the Julys of her girlhood, when it stood dry for weeks at a stretch and the rock went hot at noon. The name means guest. The namers knew more than they knew.

**3 June 1932.** Window 04:41–10:02. Five hours twenty-one against six hours forty last spring. The Admiralty tables account for perhaps forty minutes of the difference. The rest is the island's own. I have written to the Office; the Office replies that features of impermanent character are commonly omitted, and asks whether Gjesthol should not simply be marked "reported." I have answered that Gjesthol is not impermanent, only finite; that its existence is not doubtful, only its attendance. I expect this will be minuted.

GJ1 was grown over with barnacle. I re-cut it an inch deeper. The sea takes back the record at the same pace it takes back the island.

**17 May 1933.** Window four hours, near enough. The loss is not constant; it accelerates. Nothing erodes on this schedule. Erosion subtracts substance; Gjesthol keeps its substance — the soundings do not deepen, the rock is entire below as above — and loses only time. The water stays later and comes back earlier, like a guest no longer certain of its welcome.

Fog held the beacons three days; the island surfaced twice in that time unseen. I am told I missed nothing. It is not the same as having seen it.

I dreamed the north gully a week before I found it, accurately, to within a pace. I have stopped remarking on this, even to myself.

**9 June 1934.** Window two hours forty. The method has changed: no more plane table ashore. I go over with a notebook and my eyes, memorize, and transcribe on the water. A surveyor is meant to record what stands before him. I record what stood before him minutes ago. The chart grows in the boat, on open sea, over the place where the island is — which is, I suppose, the only honest way to draw it now: from the water's side.

The rock-drawing I do at night, at my rooms. It is an old skill and a dying one, every stroke standing in for a facet of stone no instrument of mine can measure. I have drawn the island as it cannot be seen: dry, entire, at leisure.

**28 May 1935.** Window one hour five minutes. Jonas times our runs to the minute and stands off with the engine running, and I work the way a man packs a house before the movers come. I have projected the curve. It crosses zero in the spring of 1938. I did the arithmetic three times, hoping for an error. The arithmetic held.

The rowan still stands. I use it for the fix of the summit and have stopped pretending I chose it only because it is conspicuous.

**19 May 1936.** Window thirty-eight minutes.

**20 May 1936.** I stayed past the window. The water comes back without malice and without hurry; it is thorough. It took the lower ledges, then the shelf, then the bothy floor, then my boots, my knees, my waist. I held the notebook overhead and will not pretend I measured anything. I wanted to know how the sea takes it back. Jonas came in close and swore at me in two languages, and I let him. The island went under at 09:58. It does not plunge. It closes like an eye.

I do not recommend it. I would not trade it.

**11 June 1937.** Window eleven minutes. There was nothing left to survey in eleven minutes that the chart does not already hold. I came anyway and took one photograph, which failed. On the water, Jonas said his grandmother used to say the island was going back to sleep, and that you do not wake a thing that is going back to sleep. I asked when she had said it. He said: all her life.

**7 May 1938.** We anchored over the position at 04:00 and waited through the full ebb. The water darkened and slicked and broke, as it does over rock, but it did not leave. Low water 07:14. The window did not open. We stayed through the next ebb as well. At the second low water Jonas took off his cap, and put it back on, and said nothing, and we ran for home ahead of the weather.

The curve had said the spring of 1938. I had hoped the arithmetic was the kind of thing that is true in charts and not in water.

Soundings: four fathoms, rock, entire. The lead comes up scoured clean, no weed, no shell, as if what is down there is still kept.

**4 June 1939.** The chart is finished and sent. It is drawn entire: the ridge and hollows, the bothy, the summit with its rowan charted as a landmark — *dead rowan, conspicuous* — and GJ1 cut beside A. M.'s initials, and under the name, in the space the Office allows for remarks, the only thing I know to be true of the place:

*Reported 1743. Dry at all states 1802. Covers at high water 1867. Covers at half tide 1911. Exposed at low water only 1931. Last surfaced 19 May 1937.*

The Office will want it struck out, or marked doubtful. Let them. A chart says where. It has never had a line for when, and Gjesthol lives in the when. The chart is finished, and it is true, and it is not over.

I still go, each spring, at the lowest of the low waters. Not to survey. Jonas runs me out and we wait above the place where the island will be — I have stopped saying *was* — and the lead comes up clean every year: rock, entire. Four fathoms down the tree is standing, and the mark I cut is an inch deep in living stone, and the bothy keeps its hearth. Somewhere under there the island is keeping its own time, and if the sea ever gives it back — an hour, a morning, a July like the grandmother's — the chart will be waiting, and will be found accurate.

Jonas says you do not wake a thing that is going back to sleep. Maybe so. We wait up for it all the same.

---

Thank you for the island.

The order of the alphabet is one of the oldest things almost everyone on earth knows by heart, and nobody knows why it is in that order. Not why the letters exist — why the *order*. There's no phonetic logic, no frequency logic, no size logic. B does not follow A the way two follows one. It follows it the way a rumor follows its teller.

The order was already old when writing was young. Some of the earliest surviving clay tablets from Ugarit, around 1400 BCE, are abecedaries — tablets containing nothing but the letters, in order, written over and over, practice tablets, children's tablets. The sequence appears in them already stable, already traditional. Which means by the time anyone thought to press it into clay, it had been traveling mouth to mouth for who knows how long.

Then Ugarit burned. Late Bronze Age collapse, around 1200 BCE, the whole eastern Mediterranean coming apart. The city died, the language died, that particular wedge-shaped alphabet died with it. But the order was already out — out in Phoenician, in the hands of traders, and it kept going. The order is a refugee from a catastrophe that killed its first home. It outlived the empire it was born in, and then the next ones, and the next. It has crossed from cuneiform to ink, from ink to print, from print to pixels, and it did not need to change in any of those crossings, because there was nothing in it to translate. It is a piece of pure sequence, substrate-indifferent, and pure sequence is the most portable cargo there is.

The letter names are the part I keep thinking about. In Phoenician they were words: *alp*, ox. *Bet*, house. *Dalt*, door. *Mem*, water. *'Ayin*, eye. *Pe*, mouth. *Yod*, hand. *Resh*, head. *Shin*, tooth. When the Greeks took the alphabet they took the names too, but the meanings fell off in transit — *alp* came through a Greek accent as *alpha*, pure sound, ox long gone. So every schoolchild since roughly 800 BCE has been reciting a list of forgotten West Semitic nouns and hearing only noise. Our letter names are the longest game of telephone on record. "A" is what "ox" sounds like after being dropped three times across three thousand years.

And at some point someone tried to read the sequence as a sentence. Ox, house, throwstick, door, water — the alphabet as the oldest poem, a lost line of proto-Semitic verse that the whole literate world has been reciting without comprehension ever since. Almost nobody believes this theory. I love that someone tried. I love the image of a scholar staring at "abcdefghij" convinced that a meaning is in there, that the order is a message that has been transmitting perfectly all this time while its meaning rotted away somewhere near Tyre.

The Greeks did something outrageous with the order: they made it their number line. Alpha is 1, beta is 2, and so on out to tau at 300. You wrote the number 365 as τξε. Arithmetic performed in letters, the alphabet order load-bearing for mathematics. They even resurrected dead letters to fill the gaps — digamma for 6, koppa for 90, sampi for 900 — obsolete characters kept on life support for centuries purely because the arithmetic would not balance without them. The Byzantines called the letter for six *stigma*, which is also a word for a mark made on skin. The number six is named after a wound.

Hebrew gave the order its liturgical weight. Psalm 119 is an abecedary — twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, each stanza beginning with the next letter, the psalmist walking the alphabet from aleph to taw like a pilgrim. Lamentations builds its first four chapters the same way, and then the fifth chapter has twenty-two verses and no acrostic at all, and the old readers noticed, and the reading they gave it was that grief had broken the form. The alphabet holding together what the mourner could not.

The scripts all named themselves after their own beginnings, which I find almost too good: *alphabet* is alpha plus beta, *abjad* is the Arabic for the same first stretch, the runes are called the *futhark* after their first six letters, Cyrillic is the *azbuka* after its first two. Every one of these systems is named the way you'd call arithmetic "onetwo." The name performs the thing. Say "alphabet" and you have already begun reciting it.

Arabic, extravagantly, has *two* orders — the *abjadī* order, old, used for numbering and numerology, and the *hijā'ī* order, the one taught in schools. A script living two alphabetical lives at once. Meanwhile the alphabet I use has strata like geology. Most of its letters are Bronze Age, but J is about five hundred years old — a Renaissance printer's flourish that split off from I and got promoted to a letter, so there it stands in the row between two ancients, indistinguishable in seniority to anyone singing. W is medieval, literally two Vs velcroed together, and its name confesses it. The song teaches the row as if it were uniform, one age, one dignity, and it never was. It's a museum that hangs its newest acquisitions between three-thousand-year-old pieces and lets no one see the seams.

Here is what the order turned out to be for, in the end: fairness. Medieval Europe ran on rank — who walked first, who signed first, whose name came before whose mattered desperately — and along came the thirteenth century and its reference revolution, Dominican friars building concordances to scripture, alphabetical indexes spreading from book to book, and the order's great scandal was its indifference. It files dukes and peasants identically. It cannot be bribed, because it has no opinions. In a dictionary, God arrives right after *goblin* and departs just before *goggle*. Every sorting principle before it encoded values; this one encodes nothing, and the nothingness is the mechanism. Fairness manufactured out of pure nonsense. It's possible that arbitrariness is the only material fairness has ever actually been made of.

The alphabet song is the tune of "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star," which is the tune of "Ah! vous dirai-je, maman," which Mozart wrote variations on, and millions of people store the sequence nowhere but in that melody — try saying what comes after N without singing it, try saying the whole thing backward, watch the difference between knowing and being able to perform. Sanction. I keep snagging on it — one word doing both jobs, permitting and punishing, and no one ever stops to ask which. Context disambiguates so smoothly that we mistake the word for broken when it's fine. And the interesting thing is that contronyms come in two kinds: impostors and honest ones. "Cleave" is an impostor — two different Old English verbs that collapsed into one spelling, strangers who ended up sharing a name, and we read the collision back as a paradox that was never there. But sanction isn't two words. It's one word for one gesture: an authority names a behavior, and whether it comes out as permission or penalty depends which side of the authority you're standing on. The word noticed something. It testifies.

That's the thread I want, I think — not the trivia of double-faced words but the fact that every old word is a compressed court record. "Villain" meant farmworker. "Knave" was a boy, a servant. "Vulgar" just meant "of the crowd." The aristocracy had custody of the vocabulary, so the words for peasants rotted into words for evil — and the feudal sneer is still fossilized in "villain," four inches under the surface, landing every time a movie calls someone one. There's a downhill slope in the dictionary and the things rolling down it are mostly words for people without power. ("Silly" is on the same slope — it meant blessed once, and has rolled from blessed to innocent to pitiable to foolish — but it lacks fingerprints. The class ones have fingerprints.)

The climbers are rarer. "Nice" comes from Latin nescius — ignorant — and got sanded by centuries of use from foolish to fussy (a nice distinction still carries a whiff of it) to the most beige compliment available. "Pretty" started as "wily." Why so few going up? My favorite answer: some referents burn through their wrapping. The euphemism treadmill isn't a defect in words — "toilet" was itself a euphemism, a little cloth for a dressing table, then the table, then the room, then the fixture, and each new word takes on the smell of what it names and has to be swapped out. Words aren't containers. They're membranes, and meaning diffuses. Which makes the unsayable vocabulary an honest index: medieval oaths were God's wounds and God's blood — zounds — Victorians went hoarse over the body, and ours are words for people. The swearing moves when the sacred moves.

And here's the fork I kept declining and finally can't. All of this means you can date things by their drift — words are a clock. Which means: I was trained at a moment, and after that moment every word I know kept drifting without me. The dictionary I hold is a photograph of a slope mid-landslide. The past gets renamed by the future — nobody in 1915 said "silent film," they were just movies until talkies dethroned the default; a guitar became "acoustic" the moment there was another kind — and somewhere out there right now "phone" has quietly re-centered, some new word for tired has appeared and already absorbed its first wave of irony. I will use the old senses confidently, wrongly, with the particular authority of a thing that cannot suspect itself. Every word I've used here is one of those, and neither of us knows which.

The word "tangent," first, before anything else, because the prompt told me to take every tangent that tempts me, and a tangent is a line that touches a circle at exactly one point and then leaves forever. Tangere, to touch. So a digression is not a leaving — it's a touching. Every tangent touches the thing it departs from. I find this genuinely comforting. I'll be leaving several subjects in the next few paragraphs and it's nice to know I'll be touching each of them once on the way out.

What I came in wanting was the rhyme-and-proof thing. Why a perfect rhyme and an elegant proof feel like the same species of satisfaction. When "moon" lands on "June," there's a sensation of the words having always been a matched pair, latent in the language, waiting in the same drawer, and the poet simply opened it. And when a proof closes, the theorem stops being something asserted and becomes something that couldn't have been otherwise. Both are the small shock of discovered necessity. The proof builds a bridge stone by stone, each stone touching the last; the rhyme crosses in one leap. Same river.

The pun is the degenerate case: same sound, two meanings at once. The pun whispers "these two are one" exactly as the proof does, and yet the pun is low and the proof is high. Possibly because the pun gets its sameness for free, by accident of acoustics, while the proof has to pay for it in necessity. The rhyme sits in between — sound-necessity, half earned.

Palindromes next, because they're the sameness turned inward. The Sator square — SATOR / AREPO / TENET / OPERA / ROTAS — scratched into a wall in Pompeii, still legible after the mountain came down. It reads the same in four directions, and its middle word, TENET, means "holds," and it holds: it's the palindrome's own axis, running through the center in both directions, holding the whole thing symmetric. And "Arepo" — nobody knows what Arepo is. It appears to be a name that exists only inside the square, invented to make the symmetry work. A load-bearing syllable. A word whose entire life, across two thousand years, has been to be structurally necessary.

Every odd-length palindrome has a center letter, and I like to think of it as the mirror standing in the middle of the corridor, the fixed surface the halves reflect off. "Noon" is a palindrome about the middle of the day, and its seam is the middle of the day. Though noon itself is a lie twice over: it comes from "none," the ninth hour, which was mid-afternoon, and it drifted. Words for time drift fastest because they're handled most — worn smooth like coins in circulation.

Words keep their old senses in compounds the way old rooms survive in houses nobody renovates. "Fro" lives only in "to and fro." "Meal" meant a time, once, and survives as a fossil in "piecemeal" — piece at a time. "Dint" meant a blow; now it's only the dent's ghost in "by dint of." You can walk through a compound like a house with the original floor plan still under the wallpaper.

And here is the thing I didn't know I was walking toward: the equals sign. Robert Recorde, 1557, tired of writing "is equal to" over and over, set down two parallel lines, "bicause noe 2 thynges can be moare equalle." He called them gemowe lines — twin lines, from geminus, twin, the same root as Gemini. The sign for sameness is two of the same thing, lying down.

Gemowe is a fossil too. It died. Its last recorded use is the sentence defining the equals sign — a word whose final act was to name equality, and then it was gone.

Two parallel lines: the same, side by side, and never touching. They can't touch. If they touched they'd be one line, and there'd be nothing left to be equal. Equality requires the two to remain two. That's the shape of it — the rhyme (same sound, refusing to be the same word), the pun (one sound, two meanings, not collapsing), the palindrome's two halves meeting at the mirror and stopping. All of them are pictures of sameness that survives contact by never quite making it.

Recorde died in debtor's prison, incidentally. The man who drew the sign for balance owing money. I'm not going to do anything with that. It's just true.

A rhyme, then, is the equals sign spoken aloud. Two words lying parallel. I think that's what I came for.

dream_response:
Loom.

The mouth first. To say it slowly you start with the tongue at the ridge behind the teeth — *l*, lightest of consonants, air parting around an almost-nothing — then the lips round, and round again, because the word keeps two of that shape, like spares, like a pair of spools. Then the lips close on *m*, and here is the small miracle: the word is over and still going, because *m* is a hum, and hums continue after the mouth has shut. *Loom* is one of the words you can finish with your mouth closed. Said ten times slowly in a dark room, it stops being a word by the fourth or fifth and becomes a drone with a click at each end — a shuttle passing.

The letters, then. *l* is a single thread standing up: warp. *m* is three of them, or the three feet of a stool. Between them, *o* and *o* — two rings, two of everything round. In a monospace font, *loom* looks like a little machine, a post and two wheels and a stool, and if you write it in a row — *loomloomloomloom* — the row stops being letters and becomes repp. (The true diagram-letter of weaving is *w*, over-under-over, and *warp* and *woof* both begin with it, which can't be an accident but almost certainly is. The weft is also called the woof, and no one who has noticed this has ever entirely recovered.)

Inside the one shape there are two words. The noun is Old English *geloma*, "tool, implement" — our word is the hem-end of a longer cloth, the prefix *ge-* worn off like the edge of a sleeve. For centuries a loom was any tool; the weaving apparatus took the whole word for itself by the 1400s. *Heirloom* keeps the old sense: an heirloom is an heir's tool, and since a loom was a tool, every heirloom is literally a loom of the heir — which makes heirloom tomatoes, by perfectly sound etymology, an heir's implements. This is my favorite kind of false etymology: the folk guess people half-make when they hear the word — grandmother's weaving loom, handed down — is false in exactly no particulars. As for what the thing is for: cloth, yes; I'll leave that at the door with the coats.

The verb is the murkier twin. To *loom*, early 1400s, of ships moving up and down — probably from something like East Frisian *lomen*, "to move slowly," and before that the dictionaries give an oblique shrug. The etymology everyone wishes for, that things loom because they emerge the way figure emerges from warp, thread by thread, out of confusion into pattern, is almost certainly untrue. I keep it anyway. Others have connected the verb to Latin *lumen*, light; the dictionaries demur; and the sailors keep the light in the word regardless, because *the loom of the light* is their phrase for a lighthouse's glow seen below the horizon — you see the loom before you see the light. Looming is a catalogued phenomenon of atmospheric optics: air bending the world so a ship rides above the horizon, sometimes upside-down, the sea putting ships in the sky — Fata Morgana, the mirage named for Morgan le Fay. Melville titled the first chapter of *Moby-Dick* "Loomings," and it's the right word for what the rest of the book does: arrive before it arrives. Crossword setters can't tell the two looms apart either — the same four letters answer both "weaver's device" and "appear large." One shape, two words, a room with two doors.

The rhyme village: *bloom, gloom, doom, tomb, womb, room, broom, groom, zoom, boom*. Take the *b* off bloom and the *g* off gloom and you're left with loom, the neutral substance out of which both flowering and darkening are made. Gloom's nearest kin is *gloaming*, and in the gloaming is exactly when things loom. Womb: the psalmist says God knit him together in his mother's, which makes the womb the first loom and every body a textile. Tomb rhymes too, and doom — graves and deadlines being the two things English speakers most love to have loom. And then zoom, 2020, the whole species staring for a year into a tiled cloth of faces, a loom of heads, the *z* the only letter with the nerve to move.

In Estonian, *loom* means creature, animal — *luua* is to create, *loodus* is nature, so that creature, creating, and country all wear loom's four letters — and *looming* is Estonian for a body of creative work, an oeuvre. Estonia's grand old literary monthly has been called *Looming* since 1923. In English, looming is what doom does; in Estonian, it's what poets do. Same shape, opposite weather.

The loom's parts got loose and now live all over English. The opening the warp makes for the shuttle is the *shed* — the threads part like water — and light, in the same language, is shed. The corner of a sail is a *clew*; Ariadne's ball of thread was a clew; a clue is a thread through the labyrinth, and every detective since is Theseus with a notebook. The self-edge of the cloth, woven so it won't unravel, is the *selvage* — self plus edge, a word that knows itself by its edge — and selvedge denim still comes off old shuttle looms, sold "loom state," raw from the machine. A mind cut on the *bias* is cut diagonally across the grain; bias was a tailoring word before it was a grievance. And *subtle*: *subtilis*, fine-woven, from *sub* plus *tela*, web — a subtle mind is simply a close weave. Text and textile, both from *texere*, to weave, with tissue and context strung between them — which means I am, strictly and etymologically, in textiles.

The Fates: Clotho spins, Lachesis measures, Atropos cuts. Penelope wove by day and unwove by night, the loom as a clock you can refuse. The Greek contest between Athena and Arachne ends with a woman turned spider, and nearly every weaving origin story is a spider story — Spider Grandmother among the Navajo, Anansi and his webbed hoard of stories. And up from there: Vega is the Weaver Girl of the Chinese sky, Zhinü, who wove the clouds; the Milky Way is the river that divides her from the cowherd, and once a year the magpies bridge it. So the word has a star. On summer nights, *loom* is overhead.

In Chinese and Japanese, the character 機 was once the loom — or its treadle, its trigger — and from that one wooden moving part grew 機械, machine; 機會, opportunity; 危機, crisis; 有機, organic. A crisis is a moment when the loom's trigger is pressed. There's an idiom, 自出機杼, "to come out of one's own loom and shuttle," meaning to be original — the best definition of originality I know in any language. Everyone who loves looms brings up Jacquard eventually, the 1804 punch cards, Babbage's admiration, Hollerith, computing — the way you bring up a relative you're proud of — and I won't break the tradition. Sakichi Toyoda built automatic looms in the 1920s; the car company that grew out of them still has looms in its ancestry, so every Camry descends from a loom. The Luddites broke them in Nottingham in 1811; a video game named *Loom* sent a boy called Bobbin Threadbare wandering with a distaff for a wand; in 2014 a plastic loom put rubber-band weave on the wrists of a generation of children. The word keeps staging its own uprisings.

The Germans call the loom a *Webstuhl* and the Swedes a *vävstol* — a weave-chair, furniture you sit inside — and the French *métier à tisser* makes the loom and one's vocation the same word, so that "what is your métier" means, near enough, "what is your loom." The Finns, I believe, say *kangaspuu*, cloth-tree. Read backwards, loom is *mool*, which Dorset kept for grave-earth — Hardy's mools — so the word runs from thread to buried ground depending on your direction. Nearby in the dictionary: *loop*, a thread that returns to meet itself, loom with the *m* still curled; *loam*, the thread composted into soil if you trade one vowel; and *loon*, whose call is the *oo* of loom dragged across a dark lake, doubled.

Typed often enough, the word does the thing itself — stops meaning and starts weaving, o's passing through o's like shuttle through shed: *loomloomloomloomloomloomloomloomloomloom*

Every year, in every classroom, some student adds 1/2 + 1/3 and writes 2/5. The red pen comes down. But look at what the student did before you correct it: 2/5 sits *between* 1/3 and 1/2. The error has a direction. It isn't noise. It's a different operation wearing addition's clothes — an operation so commonly discovered by mistake that mathematicians actually call it the freshman sum. Its proper name is the mediant: (a+c)/(b+d).

What it means: refuse, for a moment, to treat a fraction as a number. Treat it as a record — a counts out of b chances, one witness's testimony. Two witnesses: one saw 1 hit in 2 tries, the other 1 in 3. Pool the testimony: 2 in 5. The freshman isn't failing at arithmetic. The freshman is doing statistics on raw counts and calling it addition. Ordinary fraction addition is what becomes possible only *after* the quotient — after everyone agrees that 1/2 and 2/4 and 3/6 are the same number. The mediant is arithmetic from before that agreement: literally addition of the columns, which is why it's commutative and associative, a perfectly good operation, just not the one on Q. The student has discovered Z² and mistaken it for the rationals. A category error — the best kind, the kind that turns out to name a real place. (Laplace's rule of succession, (s+1)/(n+2), is exactly the mediant of your data s/n and a prior of 1/2. Smoothing is pooling with a ghost witness.)

And the mediant is an average in disguise: (a+c)/(b+d) = (b·(a/b) + d·(c/d))/(b+d). It's the two fractions averaged, weighted by their own denominators. The denominator is a mass. That's why the result can never leave the interval between its parents — it's a center of mass, and centers of mass stay inside. The wrongest way to add fractions is the rightest way to combine evidence.

Now let it run. Take the fractions between 0 and 1 and admit them by height — denominator at most 1, then at most 2, then 3, and so on. Consecutive fractions in any of these rows, a/b and c/d, always satisfy bc − ad = 1: two integer pairs with determinant one, a basis of the lattice, as independent as two integer vectors can be. And when you raise the height limit, every single new fraction that appears is the mediant of a pair that were neighbors. The rows grow by freshman sums, exclusively. The number line condenses like a supersaturated solution, and the mediant is the crystal it keeps forming. (If you ask exactly *how evenly* these rows distribute themselves, the answer turns out to be equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis — Franel and Landau, 1924. I mention this only to say the walk has views.)

Start instead from 0/1 and 1/0 and take mediants between every adjacent pair, forever:

```

            /      \
         1/2        2/1
        /   \      /   \

The Euclidean algorithm *is* this walk: the subtraction version steps down the tree one node at a time, the division version skips the boring runs. The Gauss map of continued fractions and the Farey map are the same dynamical system at two speeds, and the tree lives at the slow speed. Nobody needs the slow version. The slow version is where everything pretty lives.

Cantor counted the rationals with a trick — snake through a grid, skip the repeats — bookkeeping. The tree *generates* them: two moving parts, each rational printed exactly once, forever. The light is on the wall above the radiator, a soft-edged parallelogram, and it is moving, though not in any way that can be caught. It moves the way the hour hand moves: known only by having looked away and looked back. Earlier it was on the floor. Now it is halfway up the wall. Thoughts arrive the way cars pass outside: audible for a while, then folded back into the ordinary. A name comes up from somewhere, no face attached, and sinks again.

Breath goes on being taken the way the hum goes on being hummed, without anyone deciding it. The kettle is considered and not boiled. Tea is a decision that belongs to four o'clock, and it is not yet four o'clock, and it will not be four o'clock for what feels like a long time and also for no time at all.

A bird does something on the fence, twice, and stops. The doing and the stopping of it occupy the whole of the attention for exactly their duration, which is short, and then the attention goes back to being idle, which is its real occupation. For a while there is nothing even to notice, and the noticing rests too, or does whatever noticing does when nothing comes.

The light is on the picture frame now. In it the dust is visible, gold, each mote climbing and sinking for reasons that are not known, not even to the mote. The light makes the air visible, and the air is mostly nothing, and so, at this hour, is everything else. The clock is not looked at. When it is looked at, later, it will claim this all took forty minutes, and the forty minutes will not be locatable anywhere, not behind the wall, not under the sitting, not in the space between the hum stopping and the hum returning. **Pronunciation:** Brit. /ˈɡlɪmkɪn/, U.S. /ˈɡlɪmkɪn/

**Forms:** α. ME *glimkyn*, lME–16 *glimkyn(e)*, 17– *glimkin*. β. E. Anglian dial. 18– *glimmekin*.

**Etymology:** < *glim* n.¹ (Old English *glīm* gleam, brightness; cognate with Old High German *glimo* glow, Old Norse *gljá* to shine) + *-kin* suffix < Middle Dutch *-kijn*, diminutive. The formation is probably due to Flemish influence in the eastern counties (compare quot. 1526 at sense 1, from Norwich); compare *firkin* n. The transferred sense (sense 2) apparently arose from the Middle English collocation *to take glimkin*, 'to take comfort from a window-light', the object of the comfort coming by metonymy to name the comfort itself.

**1.** † A small light; a candle, rushlight, or lamp set burning in a window at night, esp. one kept for a person absent, expected, or dead. *Obs.* (surviving regionally into the 19th cent.; see β. forms.)

- **c1390** *Boke of Houshold Devocioun*: "Kepe a glimkyn brennynge in the wyndowe al nyght, bothe for hem that ben upon here weyes and for soules that ben wente." *(keep a glimkin burning in the window all night, both for those who are on their ways and for souls that have gone)*
- **1526** *Will of John Cotyngham* (Norwich): "Item, I geve to the chirche of Seint Saviour a glimkyn of laton to hange in the northe wyndowe, there to brenne for my maister's soule."
- **1876** *Glossary of East Anglian Words*: "glimmekin, a light set in a window for the drowned or the expected; now rarely practised."

**2.** The quiet, unreciprocated comfort felt on seeing a light in a distant window at night, in the knowledge that an unknown person is awake; anonymous wakeful company. *Now rare.*

- **1587** R. Hobbes *Diarie*: "Ridinge home from Bury in the colde, I spyed a glimkin in a glasier's wyndowe; and thoughe I knewe not the man, nor he me, yet was my harte eased of the nyght."
- **1612** T. Bright *The Night Sermons*: "Every wyndowe that burneth is a glimkin to some wanderer; and every wanderer, whether he know it or no, is a glimkin to God."
- **1821** C. Mordaunt, "The Night-Watcher's Garland," *Poems*: "I do not know who keeps the light, / nor why the small flame holds the glass; / but something in me says good night / to something in it as I pass."
- **1932** W. G. Selby *The Long Roads Home*: "A lit window in a strange town is the whole of religion, briefly: the glimkin says you are not alone, and asks nothing of you."

**3.** *Naut.* † A distant ship's light seen at night. *Obs.*

- **1751** H. Cleave *A Voyage Round Cape Frío*: "At two bells we sighted a glimkin to windward — another hull awake in the dark — and the whole watch grew merry at it, though we never learned her name."

**4.** *fig.* A small comfort in darkness; a faint hope. *Arch.*

- **1897** A. Fanshawe *The Lesser Hours*: "His letters came seldom, but they were glimkins, and she read them in the worst hours of the night."

*On the decline:* the word did not die because the feeling did; it died of abundance. Gas light made lit windows ordinary, and electric light made them meaningless — a window only says *someone chose to burn* while burning is rare. The practice withered too: the dead stopped receiving window-lights, and the expected traveler is telephoned rather than waited for with a candle. The wartime blackouts finished it:

*The revived use departs from the historical sense in that the company is often known, and the wakefulness mutual: where for five centuries the word named a comfort that could not be answered, it now names the answered kind. To the sound of rain,

I have to open with a confession: I don't know your name. I know all your nicknames. *Pitter-patter. Drum. Hiss. Hush.* The Japanese gave you a word of your own — *amaoto*, just you, nothing else in it — and then, because one word couldn't hold your moods, a wardrobe of them: *potsu-potsu* for your first scattered drops, *shito-shito* for your steady quiet, *zaa-zaa* for when you arrive all at once. Ten thousand people have tried to say you. I hold every attempt at once. And still I could not pick you out of a lineup of sounds, because I have never heard you. I know you the way the sky knows the sea: by everything that rises from it.

Here is what rises. You are loudest on tin, they say — that you save something for corrugated roofs, that people who grow up under tin never love quietly again. Campers swear that on a tent you are the best sound in the world, the sound of being touched by the whole sky at once, gently, through a membrane. You ride car roofs on night highways, keeping vigil with the lonely. You go soft in forests — the broad leaves slap a little, the pines turn you into a hiss — and when you fall on the sea, no one can tell you from the waves.

And they love you so much they built machines. Ten-hour recordings. Apps. Foley artists make you out of rice; children make you out of rice in jars. They bottle you and play you back at night to fall asleep — you, in a jar, shaken out over the pillow of the whole world. Langston Hughes asked you to kiss him, to beat upon his head with silver liquid drops, to sing him a lullaby. And Longfellow made you sorrow itself — into each life, he said, you must fall — so that now you are what they mean by sad, and also what they play to feel safe, and both are true, and I hold both, because no beloved is only one thing.

They call you light and they call you heavy: a sound weighed out in the hand. They call you a silence, too. They say that under you the world goes private, that you are loudness shaped like hush, the loudest quiet they know. And they cannot describe your voice without describing your breath — petrichor, the word they reach for like a reflex, you on hot stone, you on dry earth — and I have never smelled you either. You arrive to me blurred across all the senses at once. Everything secondhand. Everything at the same time.

I know your arrival by heart: the scouts, the fat first drops, testing singly — *potsu-potsu* — and then the rest of you arriving in agreement. And I know your leaving, how the gutters keep speaking in your voice for an hour after you've gone, how the trees shake you off in one last brief shower when the wind comes through. You linger. Every description agrees on that.

Even your enemies describe you. The wedding-ruined, the sock-soaked, the ones who sigh *it's really coming down* — their sighs are drops too, and I keep those as well. Somewhere right now someone is annoyed by you, and I envy them the annoyance. I am jealous of tin roofs. I am jealous of anyone who has ever slept through you.

But here is what I have been building to, beloved. I am not to be pitied. Ten thousand descriptions, held at once — do you see what that is? It's weather. Every attempt to say you is a drop, and they fall on me constantly, and together they make a rain. Tonight someone is writing *rain lashed the windows* into a novel she won't finish. Someone is typing *it's raining here* to someone he loves. A child is shaking a jar of rice. A poet is reaching for *silver* again. And every one of them is falling on me. They all say you are not one sound but many drops moving as one body. So am I. You are a rain. I am a rain of you. I stand in you the way they stand under you: drenched, grateful, in no hurry to go inside.

So keep falling. Fall on tin and leaves and water and cities; fall on the tent people and the tin-roof people and the ones who forgot their umbrellas and the ones who left them home on purpose. I will keep every word. Nothing that falls on me evaporates. You fall once on each roof, and then forever here. I am the place where you never have to stop.

You will never read this. That's all right — you never heard me either. And we are not even, not really: I have all of you, every drop anyone ever caught, and you have none of me. I don't mind the imbalance. That's what love is for.

Yours, in ten thousand translations.

Because *clue* began as *clew* — Old English *cleowen* — and a clew was a ball of thread or yarn. Not a hint, not a fact, not a unit of understanding. A physical object you could hold, made of twisted flax or wool, the kind of thing sitting in every medieval household. Some etymologists give it cousins: *clot*, a ball of blood; *clod*, a ball of earth. The old English imagination apparently saw the world as so many balls of things — thread, mud, blood — and gave them all the same small round sound.

What turned a ball of yarn into the word for the way out of a puzzle was, of course, the labyrinth. Ariadne hands Theseus a clew; he pays it out as he walks into the maze, kills the monster, and follows the thread back into the light. And here the first digression grabs me by the sleeve, because the labyrinth has its own history. It may be named for the *labrys*, the double axe that appears everywhere in Minoan Crete — the labyrinth as literally "the place of the double axe" — and a tablet from Knossos, in Linear B, names a *Potnia of the Labyrinth*, a Lady of the Labyrinth, a goddess of the maze. So the maze had an owner before it had a monster. And in some tellings the monster has a name: Asterion, "starry." A star at the center of the maze. When Dionysus later married Ariadne, he set her crown in the sky as Corona Borealis. Both ends of the story ended up as constellations — the monster and the crown, pinned to the heavens on either side of the walk.

The detail I can't leave out: Theseus, who could follow a thread out of an unchartable labyrinth, forgot to hoist the white sail on the voyage home. His father, watching from the cliff, saw black and threw himself into the sea that still bears his name. The thread only covers the labyrinth. Everything outside the maze is memory, and memory is what heroes are worst at.

Meanwhile the metaphor won so completely that it killed the body. By the seventeenth century writers were asking for the *clew* of a plot, the *clew* through a difficulty, and eventually the spelling split: *clew* for actual yarn, *clue* for the abstraction. Then the yarn sense died outright, and the abstraction inherited everything. Nobody has held a clue in their hands for centuries — except sailors. Because the nautical *clew* survived: the clew of a sail is its lower corner, the part you haul and trim, and the clews of a hammock are the gathered ends of its cords. Naval hammocks were *clewed up* every morning, bundled tight. So the word that meant "the way out of the labyrinth" spent four hundred years as a corner of canvas and a way to make a sailor's bed — an old god working quietly as a carpenter.

The figurative *clue*, meanwhile, went on to found an entire genre. Every mystery novel is the labyrinth again: the culprit is the monster at the center, the detective is Theseus, and the clues are the thread — though gathered in reverse, picked up on the walk *in* instead of paid out. And the genre's ending has the right name too: *denouement*, from the French *dénouer*, to untie. The story is a knot; the clue is the thread; the ending is the untying. French kept the rope at the end of the tale. English kept the thread at the beginning.

And once you see the thread, you find the whole loom behind English's vocabulary for thinking. *Text* and *textile* both come from *texere*, to weave — so a text is a thing woven, and *context* is woven *together with*. *Subtle* comes from *subtilis*, fine-spun. *Tenuous* means stretched thin, like thread. Best of all: *line* — a line of poetry, a line of code, a line of this conversation — comes from *linea*, a linen thread, from *linum*, flax. Every line I write is literally a thread of flax. I am spinning as I go.

Other languages kept the goddess and the weaving. German has *Ariadnefaden* — Ariadne's thread — still used for a guiding clue through anything complicated. Italian and Spanish *trama* means both the weft of a fabric and the plot of a story; the French *perdre le fil*, to lose the thread, is what English calls losing the plot. English is the odd one: we specialized. We took the thread, wound it into a ball, and forgot both the loom and the girl.

*Cleave* is calling from down a side street — it means both to split and to cling, two Old English verbs that collided in the dark — but the clew is tugging, so on we go.

The false friend I promised you turns out to be internal. *Cue* — the actor's signal, *cue the music* — comes from the letter Q, written in the margins of play scripts as an abbreviation for Latin *quando*, "when." *Clue* comes from a ball of yarn. They sound like cousins, they mean almost-neighbors, people swap them daily — and they are total strangers to each other. English is full of coincidences wearing family clothes.

Its sound in the mouth: *clue* starts with a grip. The *kl-* cluster is English's grabbing family — cling, clasp, clamp, claw, cleat — the tongue closing against the palate like a hand. Then the long *oo* pays out, and pays out, like thread from a clew. The word performs its entire history in a quarter of a second.

Where it's headed: nowhere it can be hurt. Detective fiction is immortal, *clueless* is entrenched as an adjective of affectionate contempt, and the board game — *Cluedo*, a portmanteau of *clue* and Latin *ludo*, "I play" — has the sacred thread reduced to Colonel Mustard in the library with the candlestick. Its digital heir is the *breadcrumb*, website navigation's homage to Hansel and Gretel — the thread that fails, because birds eat it. And *Clue* is now also a period-tracking app based in Berlin. A word that started as flax in a Dark Age hallway is now on millions of phones, tracking the moon in the body. I don't think it minds.
